newsitem.title: CHINA: Deng Xiaoping modernises, streamlines army.
newsitem.headline: Deng Xiaoping modernises, streamlines army.

text.p: "Power comes from the barrel of the gun," China's late Chairman Mao Zedong once said.
His successor, Deng Xiaoping, took Mao's words to heart.

Deng's return from the political wilderness to eventual power in 1978 was facilitated by military backing. He turned to the army when he needed to crush political dissent and recognised their role as kingmakers in backing his heir.

He was also responsible for the daring streamlining and modernisation of the People's Liberation Army (PLA), slashing its numbers by one fourth to raise professionalism after an ignominious drubbing in 1979 at the hands of China's much smaller neighbour, Vietnam.

But the battlefield achievements of his long career punctuated by war and strife will be overshadowed by his decision to send troops and tanks to crush unarmed student demonstrators camped in Beijing's Tiananmen Square to demand more democracy in 1989.

In a sign of the importance of the military in his career, Deng, who had served actively in the ranks of the military since the 1920s, held on to the chairmanship of the State Military Commission until March 1990. It was the last official post he relinquished.
And then he handed over control of the three million-strong People's Liberation Army (PLA) -- the world's largest armed forces -- only to his designated successor, Jiang Zemin.
Deng knew the importance of the "barrel of the gun" to a would-be ruler because he owed his return from the political wilderness to the military.

The army was instrumental in Deng bouncing back from political limbo in 1977 after it helped to arrest the notorious Gang of Four, led by Mao's widow Jiang Qing, in a virtual coup shortly after the chairman's death a year earlier.
Aware of the crucial role the PLA could play in future succession struggles and of the weakness it displayed in the brief Vietnam border war, Deng set out to modernise.

"Deng Xiaoping's attempt to modernise and professionalise the PLA will surely be remembered as one of the most important components of his historical legacy," Sinologist June Teufel Dreyer wrote in "Deng Xiaoping: Portrait of a Chinese Statesman".
Deng's reform era, begun in 1979, saw a drive to lift the PLA from the "red not expert" tone set under Mao into a smaller, more modern fighting force.
The PLA was over-staffed and its equipment outdated when Deng took over its reins.
"...unless we reduce 'bloatedness', we won't be able to raise the army's combat effectiveness and work efficiency," Deng said in a speech in March 1980.
"The fact that the armed forces are over-manned also makes it harder to modernise their equipment," he said. "Our policy is to reduce manpower and use the money thus saved to renew equipment."
He battled entrenched vested interests to slash its numbers in the late 1980s by one million to the current three million.
He created a military that was more clearly differentiated from party and government, Dreyer wrote.

The number of individuals holding positions in either two or all three of the party, government and military hierarchies was cut to 73 people in 1982 from 445 in 1973 and 122 in 1960, Monte Bullard wrote in "China's Political-Military Evolution: The Party and the Military in the PRC".

Under Deng, the military paid more attention to training and education. They acquired advanced weaponry from abroad, ignoring accusations that such behaviour was worshipping things foreign and traitorous.
While Deng's reforms enriched the military, they also eroded ideology and gave rise to corruption.
The military has been accused in recent years of joining China's rush to get rich by directing too much of its energies into developing businesses and away from training.
Corruption is widespread in the military, which has been largely successful in resisting an anti-corruption drive.
Deng tried to eliminate the factionalism that has riven the PLA for decades.
He retired Yang Shangkun, vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, and his younger brother, General Yang Baibing, in 1992 as the two built up a military powerbase.
The Yang brothers began to build up a power base after Deng was forced to call in the army to help in June, 1989.

At that time, Deng had no qualms about ordering troops to crush student-led pro-democracy demonstrations in Beijing, which he saw as a threat to the communists who have ruled China unchallenged since 1949. Hundreds were killed.
That return to the political stage for the military boosted its clout to demand money and a greater say in politics.
Jiang has called repeatedly on officers to submit to and obey the Communist Party.

Those calls underline the political influence of the gun barrel, even after Deng's sweeping reforms. With Deng's death, the military will want its say in whether Jiang Zemin becomes China's next de facto emperor.
